# openair-lint rules

<!-- This file is generated by "dart run tool/generate_rules_doc.dart". Do not edit it by hand. -->

openair-lint 3.0.0-dev.1 has 154 rules. Each rule has an ID, a severity and the versions of the specification that it applies to.

- **error**: the file breaks a "must" rule of the specification.
- **warning**: the file breaks a "should" rule of the specification.
- **info**: a hint about style or a recommended order.

Use `openair-lint --explain <rule-id>` to see a rule in the terminal, and `--disable <rule-id>` to turn a rule off.

39 rules have an automatic fix (column "Fix"). `openair-lint --fix` applies these fixes, and `--fix-dry-run` shows them without a change of the files. A rule fixes a problem only when there is exactly one correct result and the meaning of the file does not change. Each rule says which of its problems it fixes.

### file-not-utf8

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [general-requirements](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#general-requirements)
- Automatic fix: --fix saves a file with a UTF-16 byte order mark as UTF-8. It does not change a UTF-16 file without a byte order mark, because then the encoding is only a guess.

The file must use the UTF-8 encoding, not UTF-16.

The specification requires the UTF-8 encoding. This file uses UTF-16. Many readers cannot read UTF-16 files at all.

openair-lint finds UTF-16 from the byte order mark at the start of the file (FF FE or FE FF). It also finds UTF-16 without a byte order mark: then many characters of the text are NUL (U+0000). In this case openair-lint does not report the other problems of the header and of the commands, because it cannot read the text.

Save the file again as UTF-8. Most text editors have this option in the "Save as" dialog.

Correct:

```
(the file is saved as UTF-8)
*VERSION: 3.0
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou
```

Incorrect:

```
(the file is saved as UTF-16, it starts with the bytes FF FE)
*VERSION: 3.0
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou
```

### file-invalid-utf8

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [general-requirements](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#general-requirements)
- Automatic fix: no

The file must contain only valid UTF-8 text.

The specification requires the UTF-8 encoding. Some bytes in this file are not valid UTF-8. This usually means that the file was saved in an older 8-bit encoding, for example Windows-1252, Windows-1250 or ISO 8859-1. Readers show these characters wrongly, or they stop reading the file.

Open the file in an editor with the correct old encoding, and save it again as UTF-8. openair-lint reports one problem for each line with invalid bytes.

The message names the probable encoding (Windows-1250, 1251, 1252, 1253, 1254 or 1257), and shows the line as it reads in this encoding. This is only a guess from the bytes: check that the names are correct before you save the file. Some bytes are different letters in two encodings. For example, the byte E8 is "č" in Windows-1250 and "è" in Windows-1252. When the bytes do not show which encoding is right, the message names two encodings. openair-lint does not convert the file, because a wrong guess gives wrong letters without any error.

Correct:

```
AN München CTR      * saved as UTF-8: "ü" is the bytes C3 BC
```

Incorrect:

```
AN München CTR      * saved as Windows-1252: "ü" is the byte FC
```

### file-replacement-character

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [general-requirements](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#general-requirements)
- Automatic fix: no

The text should not contain the replacement character "�" (U+FFFD).

The character "�" (U+FFFD) replaces a character that a program could not read. When it is in a file, an earlier conversion lost the original character. For example, "München" became "M�nchen".

Write the correct character in place of "�". This rule does not report bytes that are not valid UTF-8; the rule file-invalid-utf8 reports them.

Correct:

```
AN München CTR
```

Incorrect:

```
AN M�nchen CTR
```

### file-bom

- Severity: **info**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [general-requirements](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#general-requirements)
- Automatic fix: --fix removes the byte order mark.

A UTF-8 file does not need a byte order mark (BOM).

The file starts with a UTF-8 byte order mark (the bytes EF BB BF). UTF-8 does not need it. Most readers ignore it, but some older readers see it as part of the first line. Then they do not find the "*VERSION:" header or the first command.

Save the file as "UTF-8" and not as "UTF-8 with BOM".

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 3.0
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou
* The first byte of the file is the "*" of *VERSION.
```

Incorrect:

```
﻿*VERSION: 3.0
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou
* The file starts with the bytes EF BB BF (the BOM) before *VERSION.
```

### file-mixed-line-endings

- Severity: **info**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [general-requirements](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#general-requirements)
- Automatic fix: --fix uses the most frequent line ending for all lines.

All lines should use the same line ending.

The file uses more than one kind of line ending: LF (Linux, macOS), CRLF (Windows) or CR (old Mac). This often happens when files from different sources are joined. Most readers accept it, but some tools then count the lines differently or show empty lines.

Use one kind of line ending in the whole file. Many editors can convert the line endings.

Correct:

```
AC D\n
AN Example CTR\n
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D\r\n
AN Example CTR\n
```

### file-no-airspace

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [airspace-definition](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#airspace-definition)
- Automatic fix: no

The file must contain at least one airspace definition.

An OpenAir file contains airspace definitions. Each definition starts with an "AC" command. This file has no "AC" command, so it has no airspace. It can be empty, contain only comments, or be a file of another format.

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 3.0
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou

AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
DP 46:00:00N 014:00:00E
...
```

Incorrect:

```
*VERSION: 3.0
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou
* No airspaces yet
```

### file-garbled-text

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [an-airspace-name](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#an-airspace-name)
- Automatic fix: no

A name should not contain garbled characters such as "Ã¼" in place of "ü".

Some characters in the name look like UTF-8 text that was read with a wrong encoding and then saved again. For example, "ü" became "Ã¼", and "Š" became "Å" followed by a non-breaking space. Pilots then see the garbled name.

Write the correct characters.

This rule checks the text after "AN" and "AG".

Correct:

```
AN München CTR
```

Incorrect:

```
AN MÃ¼nchen CTR
```

### file-strepla-block

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [airspace-definition](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#airspace-definition)
- Automatic fix: no

The file should not contain StrePla add-on blocks.

The program StrePla writes extra data between the comments "*$STREPLA_ADDON BEGIN" and "*$STREPLA_ADDON END", for example a colour table. The lines in the block look like commands, but they are not airspaces. The specification does not define these blocks. A reader that does not know them reads the lines as airspaces without altitude limits and without geometry.

Remove the block. openair-lint does not check the structure of the airspaces inside the block.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
...
```

Incorrect:

```
*$STREPLA_ADDON BEGIN colortable
AC A
AN COLORENTRY
SP 0 1 0x0000FF
*$STREPLA_ADDON END
```

### file-extension-not-openair

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [general-requirements](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#general-requirements)
- Automatic fix: no

The file name should end with .openair (or .txt, the legacy extension).

The specification says: use the file extension .openair, with .txt as legacy alternative. Programs and people find OpenAir files by the extension. openair-lint also searches directories only for *.openair and *.txt files.

This rule needs the name of the file. The command line tool gives it for every file. It is not checked for standard input or for text that is pasted on the web page. The extension .txt is allowed and not reported.

Correct:

```
* File name: austria.openair
AC D
...
```

Incorrect:

```
* File name: austria.dat
AC D
...
```

### header-version-missing

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [header](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#header)
- Automatic fix: no

The header must contain a "*VERSION:" comment.

Every OpenAir file must start with a header. The header must contain the version of the specification that the file follows, for example "*VERSION: 2.1". Readers use the version to understand the file. The header is the comment lines before the first command.

Version 3.0 of the specification is still a draft. The specification says that writers must not write "*VERSION: 3.0" in files before the final 3.0.0 release.

Without a version, openair-lint checks the file as version 3.0. Use the option --target 2.1 to check an older file as version 2.1.

If the file has a line such as "*VERSION 2.1" without ":", the problem is reported on that line, because readers do not see it as the version. A comment such as "* Version: MAR26" is a normal comment, because its value is not a version number.

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 2.1
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou

AC D
AN Example CTR
```

Incorrect:

```
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou

AC D
AN Example CTR
```

### header-version-invalid

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [header](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#header)
- Automatic fix: --fix removes a "V" before the number and writes a dot in place of a comma, for example "2.1" in place of "V2.1" or "2,1". It does not change other values.

The value of "*VERSION:" must be a version number, for example 2.1.

The "*VERSION:" comment must contain only the version number of the specification, for example "2.1" or "3.0". Readers cannot use other text. Write other information in a separate comment.

When the value is not a version number, openair-lint checks the file as version 3.0. Use the option --target to choose the version.

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 2.1
* Data from 2026-07-01
```

Incorrect:

```
*VERSION: 2026-07-01
```

### header-version-old

- Severity: **info**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [header](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#header)
- Automatic fix: no

Versions older than 2.1 are checked with the rules of version 2.1.

The file declares a version older than 2.1, for example "*VERSION: 2.0". openair-lint knows only the versions 2.1 and 3.0. It checks older files with the rules of version 2.1. Most rules of 2.1 also apply to older files.

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 2.1
```

Incorrect:

```
*VERSION: 2.0
```

### header-version-draft

- Severity: **info**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [header](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#header)
- Automatic fix: no

Version 3.0 is a draft. Do not write "*VERSION: 3.0" in production files yet.

The specification says: version 3.0 is a draft. Writers must not write "*VERSION: 3.0" in files before the final 3.0.0 release of the specification.

This rule is info and not an error, so that test files for the draft (for example the conformance files) can use version 3.0. Do not publish a file with "*VERSION: 3.0" before the release. The rule will be removed at the 3.0.0 release.

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 2.1
```

Incorrect:

```
*VERSION: 3.0
```

### header-version-unknown

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [header](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#header)
- Automatic fix: --fix removes the extra numbers of a known version, for example "3.0" in place of "3.0.0".

The version should be one that the specification defines: 2.1 or 3.0.

The value of "*VERSION:" is a number, but it is not a version of the specification that openair-lint knows. Examples are "2.5" (there is no such version), "3.1" (newer than this linter) and "3.0.0" (write "3.0").

openair-lint checks a version between 2.1 and 3.0 as 2.1, and a version newer than 3.0 as 3.0. Write the version exactly as the specification shows it, for example "*VERSION: 2.1".

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 3.0
```

Incorrect:

```
*VERSION: 3.0.0
```

### header-written-by-missing

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [header](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#header)
- Automatic fix: no

The header must contain a "*WRITTEN_BY:" comment.

The header must say who wrote the file: a person, an organisation or a program. Write it in a "*WRITTEN_BY:" comment, for example "*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou". This helps users to find the source of the data and to report errors.

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 2.1
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou
```

Incorrect:

```
*VERSION: 2.1
* Written by SeeYou
```

### header-written-by-empty

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [header](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#header)
- Automatic fix: no

The "*WRITTEN_BY:" comment must have a value.

The "*WRITTEN_BY:" comment is in the header, but it has no value. Write the author of the file: a person, an organisation or a program.

Correct:

```
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou
```

Incorrect:

```
*WRITTEN_BY:
```

### header-field-format

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [header](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#header)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes the line in the exact form, for example "*VERSION: 2.1" in place of "* version = 2.1".

Write header comments exactly as "*VERSION: 2.1" and "*WRITTEN_BY: Name".

The specification shows the header comments in one form: "*" at the start of the line, the key in upper case, ":" directly after the key, and one space before the value. openair-lint also reads other forms, for example "* version = 2.1", but other readers may not find the header in these forms.

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 2.1
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou
```

Incorrect:

```
* VERSION: 2.1
*Written_By:SeeYou
```

### header-field-duplicate

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [header](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#header)
- Automatic fix: --fix removes a second comment that has the same value as the first one. It does not remove a comment with another value.

The header should have only one "*VERSION:" and one "*WRITTEN_BY:" comment.

The header has the same key more than once. Readers use only one of them, and different readers can choose different ones. openair-lint uses the first one.

Keep one "*VERSION:" and one "*WRITTEN_BY:" comment. Write other information, for example other authors, in normal comments.

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 2.1
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou
* Data: Example Aero Club
```

Incorrect:

```
*VERSION: 2.1
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou
*WRITTEN_BY: Example Aero Club
```

### header-after-first-command

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [header](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#header)
- Automatic fix: no

"*VERSION:" and "*WRITTEN_BY:" belong in the header, before the first command.

The header is the comment lines at the start of the file, before the first command. A "*VERSION:" or "*WRITTEN_BY:" comment later in the file is not part of the header. Readers ignore it.

If the file already has a header, this comment is often the header of another file that was joined to this one. Remove it, or move it to the top of the file. Check that both files use the same version.

A normal comment such as "* Version: updated in May" is not reported, because its value is not a version number.

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 2.1
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou

AC D
AN Example CTR
```

Incorrect:

```
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou

AC D
*VERSION: 2.1
AN Example CTR
```

### case-not-upper-case

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 3.0
- Specification: [general-requirements](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#general-requirements)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes the command and its value in upper case. It does not change the text after AN and AG, and it does not change comments.

Commands and values must be in upper case (except the text after AN and AG, and comments).

Version 3.0 requires upper case for everything: commands, keywords, units and all other values. This includes weekdays, sun events, the letters "T" and "Z" in dates and times, and the letters "N", "S", "E" and "W" in coordinates.

Only these parts can use any case: the name after "AN", the station name after "AG", and comments (the text after "*").

openair-lint reports one problem per line, at the first lower case letter. It does not check commands that the specification does not define; other rules report them. Version 2.1 does not have this rule.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example ctr      * any case in the name
AH 1000 FT AMSL
AA MON-FRI 07:00Z/15:00Z
```

Incorrect:

```
ac D
AH 1000 ft AMSL
AA Mon-Fri 07:00z/15:00z
```

### command-outside-airspace

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [airspace-definition](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#airspace-definition)
- Automatic fix: no

Every command must be inside an airspace definition, after an AC command.

Each airspace definition must begin with the "AC" command. A command before the first "AC" command does not belong to any airspace. Readers handle such commands differently: most ignore them, some use a "V X=" command for the next airspace.

Move the command into the airspace that it belongs to, after the "AC" command. Only comments and empty lines can come before the first "AC" command.

Correct:

```
*VERSION: 3.0
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou

AC D
AN Example CTR
```

Incorrect:

```
*VERSION: 3.0
*WRITTEN_BY: SeeYou

AN Example CTR
AC D
```

### command-unknown

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [command-reference](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#command-reference)
- Automatic fix: no

Every line must be a command of the specification, a comment or an empty line.

The first word of each line is the command. This line starts with a word that is not a command of the specification. Readers do not understand the line.

Common causes are a missing space after the command (for example "AH5000 FT"), a no-break space (U+00A0) in place of a normal space after the command, a note without "*" in front of it, or a comment that starts with "#" or "//" in place of "*".

Commands of other programs, for example "SP" and "SB" of WinPilot, are reported by the rule command-not-in-spec.

Correct:

```
AH 5000 FT AMSL
* Note: changed in 2026
```

Incorrect:

```
AH5000 FT AMSL
Note: changed in 2026
```

### command-not-in-spec

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [command-reference](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#command-reference)
- Automatic fix: no

Commands of other programs (SP, SB, AT, AI, AR, TO, TC) are not part of the specification.

Some files use commands that other programs defined, for example "SP" and "SB" (pen and brush) and "AT" (label position) of WinPilot, or "AI" (airspace ID) of openAIP. This specification does not define them. Readers ignore them, or they read them in different ways.

Remove these commands. If the information is useful for people, write it in a comment.

Such commands are often on many lines. openair-lint reports each command only once per file, at its first line. The message says how many lines use it.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AF 118.480
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
SP 0,1,0,0,255
AR 118.480
```

### airspace-ac-missing

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [airspace-definition](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#airspace-definition)
- Automatic fix: no

Each airspace must begin with an AC command. Here an AC command is probably missing between two airspaces.

Each individual airspace definition must begin with the "AC" command. Readers start a new airspace only at an "AC" command.

In this airspace, the geometry is followed by a second group of "A" commands that repeats the first group (for example "AN", "AH" and "AL"), and then by more geometry. These are almost always two airspaces, and the "AC" command of the second one is missing. Readers read them as one airspace with a wrong shape, and they use only one of the names and altitude limits.

Add the "AC" command before the first "A" command of the second airspace. openair-lint reports only this problem. It does not also report the repeated "A" commands as duplicates.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN First CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
DP 46:00:00N 014:00:00E
...
AC D
AN Second CTR
AH FL95
AL 4500 FT AMSL
DP 46:30:00N 014:00:00E
...
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN First CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
DP 46:00:00N 014:00:00E
...
AN Second CTR
AH FL95
AL 4500 FT AMSL
DP 46:30:00N 014:00:00E
...
```

### airspace-ah-missing

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ah-upper-altitude-limit](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ah-upper-altitude-limit)
- Automatic fix: no

Every airspace must have an "AH" command (the upper limit).

Each airspace definition needs exactly one upper limit ("AH") and one lower limit ("AL"). This airspace has no "AH" command. Readers then guess the upper limit, and different readers guess differently.

Add the "AH" command after the "AC" command. Use "AH UNL" if the airspace has no upper limit.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
DP 46:00:00N 014:00:00E
...
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AL GND
DP 46:00:00N 014:00:00E
...
```

### airspace-al-missing

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [al-lower-altitude-limit](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#al-lower-altitude-limit)
- Automatic fix: no

Every airspace must have an "AL" command (the lower limit).

Each airspace definition needs exactly one upper limit ("AH") and one lower limit ("AL"). This airspace has no "AL" command. Readers then guess the lower limit, and different readers guess differently.

Add the "AL" command after the "AC" command. Use "AL GND" if the airspace starts at the ground.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
DP 46:00:00N 014:00:00E
...
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
DP 46:00:00N 014:00:00E
...
```

### airspace-ah-duplicate

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ah-upper-altitude-limit](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ah-upper-altitude-limit)
- Automatic fix: no

An airspace must have only one "AH" command.

Each airspace definition must include only one upper limit. With two "AH" commands, the airspace is ambiguous: some readers use the first one and others use the last one.

Keep one "AH" command. If the airspace really has two parts with different limits, write two airspace definitions.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AH FL95
```

### airspace-al-duplicate

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [al-lower-altitude-limit](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#al-lower-altitude-limit)
- Automatic fix: no

An airspace must have only one "AL" command.

Each airspace definition must include only one lower limit. With two "AL" commands, the airspace is ambiguous: some readers use the first one and others use the last one.

Keep one "AL" command. If the airspace really has two parts with different limits, write two airspace definitions.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AL GND
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AL GND
AL 1000 FT AGL
```

### airspace-geometry-missing

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [command-reference](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#command-reference)
- Automatic fix: no

Every airspace must have a geometry (DP, DA, DB, DC or DY commands).

Each airspace must have at least one geometry command: "DP", "DA", "DB", "DC" or "DY". A "V" command alone is not a geometry. This airspace has no geometry command, so it has no shape. Readers cannot show it, and most of them ignore it.

Add the geometry, or remove the airspace.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
V X=46:00:00N 014:00:00E
DC 5
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
V X=46:00:00N 014:00:00E
```

### airspace-attribute-duplicate

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 3.0
- Specification: [command-reference](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#command-reference)
- Automatic fix: no

An airspace must have at most one AN, AY, AG and AX command.

Each airspace can have at most one "AN" (name), "AY" (type), "AG" (station) and "AX" (transponder code) command. When a command is in the same airspace two times, readers use only one of the values, and different readers use different ones. Some readers even start a new airspace at the second "AN".

Keep one command. If the lines are two airspaces, start the second one with its own "AC" command.

"AF" can be used more than once: write one "AF" command for each frequency. "AH" and "AL" have their own rules (airspace-ah-duplicate and airspace-al-duplicate).

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AF 118.480
AF 120.500
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AN Example TMA
AF 118.480
```

### airspace-attribute-duplicate-v21

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1
- Specification: [command-reference](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#command-reference)
- Automatic fix: no

An airspace should have at most one AN, AY, AG and AX command (version 2.1).

Each airspace can have at most one "AN" (name), "AY" (type), "AG" (station) and "AX" (transponder code) command. When a command is in the same airspace two times, readers use only one of the values, and different readers use different ones. Some readers even start a new airspace at the second "AN".

Keep one command. If the lines are two airspaces, start the second one with its own "AC" command.

"AF" can be used more than once: write one "AF" command for each frequency. "AH" and "AL" have their own rules (airspace-ah-duplicate and airspace-al-duplicate).

The version 2.1 text does not have this rule. Version 3.0 has it, and there it is an error (airspace-attribute-duplicate). A reader of a 2.1 file has the same problem, so openair-lint reports a warning in version 2.1 files.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AF 118.480
AF 120.500
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AN Example TMA
AF 118.480
```

### airspace-command-order

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [airspace-definition](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#airspace-definition)
- Automatic fix: no

The "A" commands should come before the geometry (D and V commands).

An airspace definition starts with "AC" and the other "A" commands. The geometric definition with "D" and "V" commands follows them. Some readers stop reading the "A" commands of an airspace when the geometry starts. For example, a reader can start a new airspace at an "AN" command after the geometry.

Move all "A" commands before the first "D" or "V" command. openair-lint reports this once per airspace, at the first "A" command after the geometry.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
V X=46:00:00N 014:00:00E
DC 5
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
V X=46:00:00N 014:00:00E
DC 5
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
```

### airspace-an-missing

- Severity: **info**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [an-airspace-name](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#an-airspace-name)
- Automatic fix: no

An airspace usually has a name (AN).

The "AN" command is optional, but pilots need the name to know which airspace a reader shows or warns about. Add an "AN" command with the name of the airspace.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AH 4500 FT AMSL
```

### airspace-duplicate

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [airspace-definition](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#airspace-definition)
- Automatic fix: no

The same airspace should not be in the file two times.

Two airspace definitions in the file have the same commands: the same class, name, limits, activation times and geometry. Readers show the airspace two times and can warn two times. This often happens when files are joined.

Remove one of them. The comparison ignores case, blanks, comments and commands that the specification does not define.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
V X=46:00:00N 014:00:00E
DC 5
AC D
AN Example TMA
AH FL95
AL 4500 FT AMSL
V X=46:00:00N 014:00:00E
DC 10
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
V X=46:00:00N 014:00:00E
DC 5
AC D
AN Example CTR
AH 4500 FT AMSL
AL GND
V X=46:00:00N 014:00:00E
DC 5
```

### ac-class-missing

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ac-airspace-class](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ac-airspace-class)
- Automatic fix: no

The AC command must contain an airspace class.

Every airspace starts with an AC command, and the AC command contains the class of the airspace. The classes are A, B, C, D, E, F, G and UNC. Use UNC if the airspace has no class or the class is not known.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
```

Incorrect:

```
AC
AN Example CTR
```

### ac-unknown-class

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ac-airspace-class](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ac-airspace-class)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes "UNC" in place of an old word for "unclassified": UNCLASSIFIED, UNCL, UNK, UKN or UNKNOWN. It does not change other values.

The AC class must be A, B, C, D, E, F, G or UNC.

AC contains only the airspace class. The classes are A, B, C, D, E, F, G and UNC (unclassified).

Old OpenAir files also use AC for the type of the airspace, for example "AC R" for a restricted area or "AC CTR" for a control zone. The specification does not allow this. Write the class in AC and the type in AY. If the class is not known, write "AC UNC".

Correct:

```
AC UNC
AY R
AN Example restricted area
```

Incorrect:

```
AC R
AN Example restricted area
```

### ay-type-missing

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ay-airspace-type](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ay-airspace-type)
- Automatic fix: no

The AY command must contain an airspace type.

AY gives the type of the airspace, for example "AY CTR" or "AY R". An AY command without a type has no meaning. Write a type from the table in the specification, write "AY NONE" for an airspace without a type, or remove the AY command.

Correct:

```
AC D
AY CTR
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AY
```

### ay-unknown-type

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ay-airspace-type](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ay-airspace-type)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes the type of the table in place of a word with the same meaning, for example "R" in place of "RESTRICTED" and "GSEC" in place of "GLIDING_SECTOR". It does not change a value when the type is only a guess.

The AY type must be a type from the table in the specification.

AY accepts only the types in the table of the specification, for example CTR, TMA, RMZ, TMZ, R (restricted), Q (danger), P (prohibited) or GSEC (gliding sector). Use NONE for an airspace without a type. A reader does not understand other values.

Old files sometimes use long names, for example "RESTRICTED" in place of "R". openair-lint suggests the type from the table when it can.

Correct:

```
AC UNC
AY R
```

Incorrect:

```
AC UNC
AY RESTRICTED
```

### ay-not-after-ac

- Severity: **info**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ay-airspace-type](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ay-airspace-type)
- Automatic fix: no

AY is usually written directly after the AC command.

The specification says that AY is typically used immediately after the AC command. The class and the type together describe the airspace, so they are easier to read on two lines next to each other. The order does not change the meaning.

Correct:

```
AC E
AY RMZ
AN Example RMZ
```

Incorrect:

```
AC E
AN Example RMZ
AY RMZ
```

### an-name-empty

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [an-airspace-name](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#an-airspace-name)
- Automatic fix: no

The AN command must contain a name.

AN gives the name of the airspace. Pilots see this name on the map and in warnings. An AN command without a name has no meaning. Write the name, or remove the AN command.

Correct:

```
AC D
AN Example CTR
```

Incorrect:

```
AC D
AN
```

### an-name-too-long

- Severity: **info**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [an-airspace-name](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#an-airspace-name)
- Automatic fix: no

The AN name is very long (more than 100 characters).

Pilots read the name on small screens. A very long name is hard to show and hard to read. Very long names often contain data that belongs in other commands: put the frequency in AF, the station name in AG, the altitudes in AH and AL, and the activation times in AA.

The specification has no limit for the length. openair-lint reports names with more than 100 characters.

Correct:

```
AN TSA EXAMPLE 22
AF 135.630
```

Incorrect:

```
AN TSA EXAMPLE 22 135.63 125.00 125.78 129.65 132.125 129.425 134.455 135.80 122.575 128.275 131.275 133.615 255.70 121.50
```

### an-contains-asterisk

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 3.0
- Specification: [an-airspace-name](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#an-airspace-name)
- Automatic fix: no

An AN line must not contain "*". The "*" starts a comment, and a comment is not allowed on the same line as AN.

The "*" character always starts a comment, and the comment runs to the end of the line. For this reason, the name after AN cannot contain "*", and a comment is not allowed on the same line as AN. A reader shows only the text before the "*" as the name.

If the "*" is part of the name, remove the "*" characters. If the text after the "*" is a comment, put the comment on its own line, before or after the AN line.

In version 2.1 files this is a warning (an-contains-asterisk-v21).

Correct:

```
* part in France
AN EKR664 ZONE 1 (NOTAM)
```

Incorrect:

```
AN EKR664 ZONE 1 (*NOTAM*) * part in France
```

### an-contains-asterisk-v21

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1
- Specification: [seeyou-openair-file-format-specification](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/v2.1.5/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#seeyou-openair-file-format-specification)
- Automatic fix: no

An AN line should not contain "*" (version 2.1). The "*" starts a comment, so readers cut the name there.

The version 2.1 text says: a comment begins with "*" and extends to the end of the line. So also in a version 2.1 file, a reader shows only the text before the "*" as the name.

If the "*" is part of the name, remove the "*" characters. If the text after the "*" is a comment, put the comment on its own line, before or after the AN line.

Version 3.0 also says that the name cannot contain "*" and that a comment is not allowed on the same line as AN. In version 3.0 this is an error (an-contains-asterisk).

Correct:

```
* part in France
AN EKR664 ZONE 1 (NOTAM)
```

Incorrect:

```
AN EKR664 ZONE 1 (*NOTAM*) * part in France
```

### af-invalid-format

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [af-airspace-frequency](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#af-airspace-frequency)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes a dot in place of a decimal comma ("123.300" in place of "123,300"), and removes the unit MHz ("123.300" in place of "123.300 MHz"). It does not change other values.

The AF frequency must be one number in MHz, with a dot as the decimal separator and without a unit.

AF gives the radio frequency that pilots use for this airspace. Write one frequency in MHz, with a dot as the decimal separator and without a unit, for example "AF 123.300". A reader cannot use a value with a comma, a unit, letters or more than one frequency.

If the airspace has more than one frequency, write one AF command for each frequency. Put the name of the radio station in AG, not in AF.

Correct:

```
AF 123.300
AG Example Information
```

Incorrect:

```
AF 123,300 MHz
```

### af-outside-air-band

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 3.0
- Specification: [af-airspace-frequency](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#af-airspace-frequency)
- Automatic fix: no

The AF frequency must be in the VHF air band (118.000 to 136.990 MHz).

The specification requires a channel in the VHF air band, from 118.000 to 136.990 MHz. Glider pilots use VHF radios. A frequency outside this band is usually a mistake, for example a navigation frequency (VOR) or a military UHF frequency, or the value is in kHz and not in MHz.

Correct:

```
AF 123.300
```

Incorrect:

```
AF 114.880
```

### af-outside-air-band-v21

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1
- Specification: [af-airspace-frequency](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#af-airspace-frequency)
- Automatic fix: no

The AF frequency should be in the VHF air band (118.000 to 136.990 MHz) (version 2.1).

The specification requires a channel in the VHF air band, from 118.000 to 136.990 MHz. Glider pilots use VHF radios. A frequency outside this band is usually a mistake, for example a navigation frequency (VOR) or a military UHF frequency, or the value is in kHz and not in MHz.

The version 2.1 text does not have this rule. Version 3.0 has it, and there it is an error (af-outside-air-band). A reader of a 2.1 file has the same problem, so openair-lint reports a warning in version 2.1 files.

Correct:

```
AF 123.300
```

Incorrect:

```
AF 114.880
```

### af-invalid-channel

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 3.0
- Specification: [af-airspace-frequency](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#af-airspace-frequency)
- Automatic fix: no

The AF frequency must be a valid 25 kHz or 8.33 kHz channel name.

Pilots set a channel name on the radio, for example 118.005 or 123.455. With 25 kHz and 8.33 kHz channel spacing, not every value is a channel. The last two digits of a channel name are 00, 05, 10, 15, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50, 55, 60, 65, 75, 80, 85 or 90. Other values, for example 118.020 or 123.456, are not channels that a radio can use.

A value with two decimals that ends in 2 or 7, for example 122.47, is often a 25 kHz frequency with the last digit cut off (122.475).

A value with more than three decimals that is the exact radio frequency of a channel (within 1 kHz), for example 118.0083 for the channel 118.010, is reported by af-not-three-decimals. Other values with more than three decimals, for example 123.4567, are reported here.

Correct:

```
AF 122.475
```

Incorrect:

```
AF 122.47
```

### af-invalid-channel-v21

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1
- Specification: [af-airspace-frequency](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#af-airspace-frequency)
- Automatic fix: no

The AF frequency should be a valid 25 kHz or 8.33 kHz channel name (version 2.1).

Pilots set a channel name on the radio, for example 118.005 or 123.455. With 25 kHz and 8.33 kHz channel spacing, not every value is a channel. The last two digits of a channel name are 00, 05, 10, 15, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50, 55, 60, 65, 75, 80, 85 or 90. Other values, for example 118.020 or 123.456, are not channels that a radio can use.

A value with two decimals that ends in 2 or 7, for example 122.47, is often a 25 kHz frequency with the last digit cut off (122.475).

A value with more than three decimals that is the exact radio frequency of a channel (within 1 kHz), for example 118.0083 for the channel 118.010, is reported by af-not-three-decimals. Other values with more than three decimals, for example 123.4567, are reported here.

The version 2.1 text does not have this rule. Version 3.0 has it, and there it is an error (af-invalid-channel). A reader of a 2.1 file has the same problem, so openair-lint reports a warning in version 2.1 files.

Correct:

```
AF 122.475
```

Incorrect:

```
AF 122.47
```

### af-not-three-decimals

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 3.0
- Specification: [af-airspace-frequency](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#af-airspace-frequency)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes the frequency with three decimals, for example "126.100" in place of "126.1" or "126.1000". It does not change a radio frequency such as 118.0083 to a channel name.

The AF frequency must have exactly three decimals.

The specification requires one number with a dot and exactly three decimals, for example "AF 123.300" or "AF 118.005". With 8.33 kHz channel spacing, three decimals are necessary to show the channel. Write "AF 126.100", not "AF 126.1" or "AF 126.1000".

Write the channel name that pilots set on the radio, not the exact radio frequency. For example, write 118.010, not 118.0083.

Version 2.1 did not define the number of decimals, so this rule applies only to version 3.0.

Correct:

```
AF 126.100
```

Incorrect:

```
AF 126.1
```

### ag-station-empty

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ag-station-name](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ag-station-name)
- Automatic fix: no

The AG command must contain a station name.

AG gives the name of the radio station that controls the airspace, as a pilot says it in a radio call, for example "AG Nordholz Radar". An AG command without a name has no meaning. Write the name, or remove the AG command.

Correct:

```
AF 123.300
AG Nordholz Radar
```

Incorrect:

```
AF 123.300
AG
```

### ag-station-is-frequency

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ag-station-name](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ag-station-name)
- Automatic fix: no

The AG station name should be a name, not a frequency.

AG gives the name of the radio station, for example "AG Nordholz Radar". The frequency belongs in AF. A reader shows the AG text as the name of the station.

The specification does not forbid numbers in AG. openair-lint reports a warning because a frequency in AG is almost always a mistake.

Correct:

```
AF 118.655
AG Vamdrup Information
```

Incorrect:

```
AG 118.655
```

### ag-contains-asterisk

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 3.0
- Specification: [ag-station-name](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ag-station-name)
- Automatic fix: no

An AG line must not contain "*". The "*" starts a comment, and a comment is not allowed on the same line as AG.

The "*" character always starts a comment, and the comment runs to the end of the line. For this reason, the station name after AG cannot contain "*", and a comment is not allowed on the same line as AG. A reader shows only the text before the "*" as the station name.

If the "*" is part of the station name, remove the "*" characters. If the text after the "*" is a comment, put the comment on its own line, before or after the AG line.

In version 2.1 files this is a warning (ag-contains-asterisk-v21).

Correct:

```
* only in summer
AG Langen Information (FIS)
```

Incorrect:

```
AG Langen Information (*FIS*) * only in summer
```

### ag-contains-asterisk-v21

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1
- Specification: [seeyou-openair-file-format-specification](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/v2.1.5/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#seeyou-openair-file-format-specification)
- Automatic fix: no

An AG line should not contain "*" (version 2.1). The "*" starts a comment, so readers cut the station name there.

The version 2.1 text says: a comment begins with "*" and extends to the end of the line. So also in a version 2.1 file, a reader shows only the text before the "*" as the station name.

If the "*" is part of the station name, remove the "*" characters. If the text after the "*" is a comment, put the comment on its own line, before or after the AG line.

Version 3.0 also says that the station name cannot contain "*" and that a comment is not allowed on the same line as AG. In version 3.0 this is an error (ag-contains-asterisk).

Correct:

```
* only in summer
AG Langen Information (FIS)
```

Incorrect:

```
AG Langen Information (*FIS*) * only in summer
```

### ax-not-four-digits

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ax-transponder-code](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ax-transponder-code)
- Automatic fix: no

The AX transponder code must have exactly 4 digits.

AX gives the transponder code (squawk) for the airspace. The specification requires a code with exactly 4 digits, for example "AX 7000". Write all 4 digits, also the zeros at the start: write "AX 0424", not "AX 424". Do not add other text.

Correct:

```
AX 0424
```

Incorrect:

```
AX 424
```

### ax-not-octal

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 3.0
- Specification: [ax-transponder-code](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ax-transponder-code)
- Automatic fix: no

The AX transponder code must use only the digits 0 to 7.

Transponder codes are octal. Each of the 4 digits is from 0 to 7, so there are 4096 codes, from 0000 to 7777. The digits 8 and 9 are not allowed. A transponder cannot be set to a code with the digit 8 or 9.

Correct:

```
AX 4410
```

Incorrect:

```
AX 4810
```

### ax-not-octal-v21

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1
- Specification: [ax-transponder-code](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ax-transponder-code)
- Automatic fix: no

The AX transponder code should use only the digits 0 to 7 (version 2.1).

Transponder codes are octal. Each of the 4 digits is from 0 to 7, so there are 4096 codes, from 0000 to 7777. The digits 8 and 9 are not allowed. A transponder cannot be set to a code with the digit 8 or 9.

The version 2.1 text does not have this rule. Version 3.0 has it, and there it is an error (ax-not-octal). A reader of a 2.1 file has the same problem, so openair-lint reports a warning in version 2.1 files.

Correct:

```
AX 4410
```

Incorrect:

```
AX 4810
```

### ax-emergency-code

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ax-transponder-code](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ax-transponder-code)
- Automatic fix: no

The AX transponder code should not be an emergency code (7500, 7600 or 7700).

The codes 7500 (unlawful interference), 7600 (radio failure) and 7700 (emergency) have a special meaning everywhere. An airspace never asks pilots to use them. Such a code in AX is a mistake.

The specification does not list these codes. openair-lint reports a warning because such a code is almost always a mistake.

Correct:

```
AX 7000
```

Incorrect:

```
AX 7700
```

## Altitude limits (AH, AL)

| Rule | Severity | Versions | Fix | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`altitude-empty`](#altitude-empty) | error | 2.1, 3.0 |  | AH and AL must have a value. |
| [`altitude-invalid`](#altitude-invalid) | error | 2.1, 3.0 | yes | The altitude must have one of the forms of the specification. |
| [`altitude-legacy-keyword`](#altitude-legacy-keyword) | error | 2.1, 3.0 | yes | Write "GND" and "UNL", not old forms such as "SFC" or "UNLIM". |
| [`altitude-gnd-in-ah`](#altitude-gnd-in-ah) | error | 2.1, 3.0 |  | GND is only allowed in AL, not in AH. |
| [`altitude-unl-in-al`](#altitude-unl-in-al) | error | 2.1, 3.0 |  | UNL is only allowed in AH, not in AL. |
| [`altitude-unit-missing`](#altitude-unit-missing) | error | 2.1, 3.0 | yes | An altitude must have the unit FT or M. |
| [`altitude-unknown-unit`](#altitude-unknown-unit) | error | 2.1, 3.0 | yes | The unit of an altitude must be FT or M. |
| [`altitude-reference-missing`](#altitude-reference-missing) | error | 2.1, 3.0 |  | An altitude must have the reference AMSL, AGL or STD. |
| [`altitude-unknown-reference`](#altitude-unknown-reference) | error | 2.1, 3.0 | yes | The altitude reference must be AMSL, AGL or STD. |
| [`altitude-msl-alias`](#altitude-msl-alias) | warning | 2.1, 3.0 | yes | Write "AMSL", not "MSL". |
| [`altitude-multiple-values`](#altitude-multiple-values) | error | 2.1, 3.0 |  | AH and AL must have only one altitude. |
| [`altitude-flight-level-invalid`](#altitude-flight-level-invalid) | error | 2.1, 3.0 | yes | A flight level must be "FL" and a whole number, for example "FL95". |
| [`altitude-flight-level-space`](#altitude-flight-level-space) | warning | 2.1, 3.0 | yes | Write a flight level without a space: "FL95", not "FL 95". |
| [`altitude-unit-no-space`](#altitude-unit-no-space) | error | 3.0 | yes | Write a space between the number and the unit. |
| [`altitude-spacing`](#altitude-spacing) | info | 2.1, 3.0 | yes | Use one space between the parts of an altitude. |
| [`altitude-out-of-range`](#altitude-out-of-range) | warning | 2.1, 3.0 |  | An altitude should be a realistic value. |
| [`altitude-zero-agl`](#altitude-zero-agl) | warning | 2.1, 3.0 | yes | For a lower limit at the ground, write "AL GND". |
| [`altitude-lower-not-below-upper`](#altitude-lower-not-below-upper) | error | 2.1, 3.0 |  | The lower limit (AL) must be below the upper limit (AH). |
| [`altitude-unit-metres`](#altitude-unit-metres) | info | 2.1, 3.0 |  | Feet (FT) are recommended for altitudes. Metres (M) are allowed. |

### altitude-empty

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [a-altitude-definitions](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#a-altitude-definitions)
- Automatic fix: no

AH and AL must have a value.

An AH or AL command without a value does not define a limit. Write the altitude after the command.

Correct:

```
AH FL95
AL GND
```

Incorrect:

```
AH
AL GND
```

### altitude-invalid

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [altitude](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#altitude)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes a normal space in place of a special space character, and removes a thousands separator ("5000" in place of "5,000" or "5 000"). It does not change other values.

The altitude must have one of the forms of the specification.

An altitude has one of these forms:

- a flight level: "FL95",
- a number, a unit and a reference: "1000 FT AMSL", "300 M AGL" or "9500 FT STD",
- "GND" for a lower limit at the ground (AL only),
- "UNL" for no upper limit (AH only).

This rule reports values that do not have one of these forms, for example "NOTAM", and text after a valid altitude. A file must contain the limit itself. A reader must not need a NOTAM or other information outside the file to understand it.

The rule also reports these problems:

- a thousands separator in the number: write "5000", not "5,000" or "5 000",
- a number that is not a plain number, for example "1,5",
- a unit or a reference that is written two times,
- other characters between the parts, for example "1000 (FT) AMSL",
- a special space character, such as the no-break space U+00A0. Use a normal space.

Correct:

```
AH FL95
AL 1000 FT AMSL
```

Incorrect:

```
AH NOTAM
AL 1000 FT AMSL (SFC)
```

### altitude-legacy-keyword

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [supported-altitude-references](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#supported-altitude-references)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes "GND" or "UNL" in place of the old word, for example "GND" in place of "SFC". It does not change "SFC" in AH or "UNLIM" in AL.

Write "GND" and "UNL", not old forms such as "SFC" or "UNLIM".

Old files use other words for the ground and for no upper limit, for example "SFC", "AGL" alone, "UNLIM" or "UNLTD". The specification defines only "GND" (AL only) and "UNL" (AH only). Some readers do not understand the other words.

Correct:

```
AH UNL
AL GND
```

Incorrect:

```
AH UNLIM
AL SFC
```

### altitude-gnd-in-ah

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [supported-altitude-references](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#supported-altitude-references)
- Automatic fix: no

GND is only allowed in AL, not in AH.

GND means "at the ground". It is only allowed as a lower limit (AL). An upper limit (AH) at the ground makes an airspace without height.

Often the upper and lower limits are swapped, or the upper limit is a height above the ground, such as "1000 FT AGL".

Correct:

```
AH 1000 FT AGL
AL GND
```

Incorrect:

```
AH GND
AL 1000 FT AGL
```

### altitude-unl-in-al

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [supported-altitude-references](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#supported-altitude-references)
- Automatic fix: no

UNL is only allowed in AH, not in AL.

UNL means "no upper limit". It is only allowed as an upper limit (AH). A lower limit (AL) cannot be unlimited.

Often the upper and lower limits are swapped.

Correct:

```
AH UNL
AL FL195
```

Incorrect:

```
AH FL195
AL UNL
```

### altitude-unit-missing

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [altitude](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#altitude)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes "AL GND" for a lower limit of 0 above the ground without a unit, for example "AL 0 AGL". It does not add a unit to other values, because FT and M are both possible.

An altitude must have the unit FT or M.

An altitude has a number, a unit and a reference. The unit is required: FT (feet) or M (metres). Feet are recommended. An altitude without a unit is not valid, for example "1000 AMSL". Without the unit, a reader does not know if the number is in feet or in metres. The meaning of a file must not depend on the settings of the reader.

A flight level ("FL95") has no unit. A value of 0 also needs a unit. For "AL 0 AGL", the message says to write "AL GND", because this is the form of the specification for a lower limit at the ground.

Correct:

```
AH 3500 FT AMSL
AL 1000 FT AGL
```

Incorrect:

```
AH 3500 AMSL
AL 1000 AGL
```

### altitude-unknown-unit

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [altitude](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#altitude)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes "FT" or "M" in place of an old unit word, for example "FT" in place of "FEET" or "F".

The unit of an altitude must be FT or M.

The specification defines two units for altitudes: FT (feet, recommended) and M (metres). Other forms, such as "F" or "FEET", are not valid.

Correct:

```
AH 3500 FT AMSL
```

Incorrect:

```
AH 3500 F AMSL
```

### altitude-reference-missing

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [altitude](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#altitude)
- Automatic fix: no

An altitude must have the reference AMSL, AGL or STD.

The format of AH and AL is "Altitude Unit AltRef": the number, the unit and the altitude reference. The reference is required. It says what the altitude is measured from:

- AMSL: above mean sea level,
- AGL: above ground level,
- STD: standard pressure (a pressure altitude, like a flight level).

An altitude without a reference is not valid, for example "1000 FT". Without the reference, readers guess. Most of them use AMSL, but this is not certain. A flight level ("FL95"), "GND" and "UNL" have no reference.

Correct:

```
AH 3500 FT AMSL
```

Incorrect:

```
AH 3500 FT
```

### altitude-unknown-reference

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [supported-altitude-references](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#supported-altitude-references)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes the reference of the specification in place of an old word: AMSL for ASL, ALT and QNH, AGL for GND, SFC and ASFC after a number, and STD for QNE. For "AL 0 FT GND" it writes "AL GND". It does not change a word that is not known.

The altitude reference must be AMSL, AGL or STD.

The specification defines the altitude references AMSL, AGL and STD, and the flight level form "FL95". Old files use other words, for example "ASL" or "ALT" for AMSL, and "GND" or "SFC" for AGL. Some readers do not understand them.

Note: "1000 FT GND" is a height above the ground. Write it as "1000 FT AGL". "GND" alone (without a number) is the correct form for a lower limit at the ground.

"MSL" is an alias of AMSL that the specification allows. The rule altitude-msl-alias reports it.

Correct:

```
AH 3500 FT AMSL
AL 1000 FT AGL
```

Incorrect:

```
AH 3500 FT ASL
AL 1000 FT GND
```

### altitude-msl-alias

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [supported-altitude-references](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#supported-altitude-references)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes "AMSL" in place of "MSL".

Write "AMSL", not "MSL".

"MSL" is an alias of "AMSL" (above mean sea level). A reader must read "MSL" as "AMSL", so the meaning is the same. But writers should write "AMSL". openair-lint reads "MSL" as AMSL for all other checks, for example to compare the lower and the upper limit.

Correct:

```
AH 3500 FT AMSL
```

Incorrect:

```
AH 3500 FT MSL
```

### altitude-multiple-values

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [ah-upper-altitude-limit](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#ah-upper-altitude-limit)
- Automatic fix: no

AH and AL must have only one altitude.

Each airspace definition must include only one upper limit and only one lower limit. A value with two altitudes, for example "100 M AGL/423 M AMSL", is ambiguous and not permitted. Readers handle it in different ways.

Write the one limit that applies. You can put the other value in a comment.

Correct:

```
AH 423 M AMSL * 100 M AGL
```

Incorrect:

```
AH 100 M AGL/423 M AMSL
```

### altitude-flight-level-invalid

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [altitude](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#altitude)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes "FL95" in place of "95 FL", and removes FT or STD after a flight level ("FL95" in place of "FL95 FT"). It does not change other values.

A flight level must be "FL" and a whole number, for example "FL95".

A flight level is written as "FL" and a whole number, without a unit and without a reference. "FL95" means 9500 feet at standard pressure. Decimals ("FL95.5"), a number before "FL" ("95 FL") and a unit after the flight level ("FL95 FT") are not valid.

For a pressure altitude that is not a whole flight level, use STD: "9550 FT STD".

Correct:

```
AH FL95
```

Incorrect:

```
AH FL95.5
```

### altitude-flight-level-space

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [supported-altitude-references](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#supported-altitude-references)
- Automatic fix: --fix removes the space: "FL95" in place of "FL 95".

Write a flight level without a space: "FL95", not "FL 95".

"FL 145" (with a space) has the same meaning as "FL145". A reader must accept it, but writers should write "FL145", without a space. openair-lint reads "FL 145" as FL145 for all other checks.

Correct:

```
AH FL145
```

Incorrect:

```
AH FL 145
```

### altitude-unit-no-space

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 3.0
- Specification: [altitude](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#altitude)
- Automatic fix: --fix adds the space: "1000 FT" in place of "1000FT".

Write a space between the number and the unit.

In version 3.0, an altitude has a space between the number and the unit: "1000 FT", not "1000FT". Version 2.1 allowed both forms.

Correct:

```
AL 1000 FT AMSL
```

Incorrect:

```
AL 1000FT AMSL
```

### altitude-spacing

- Severity: **info**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [altitude](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#altitude)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes one space between the parts.

Use one space between the parts of an altitude.

Write exactly one space between the number, the unit and the reference. Two or more spaces, or a tab, make the file harder to read and to compare.

Correct:

```
AH 1000 FT AMSL
```

Incorrect:

```
AH 1000  FT   AMSL
```

### altitude-out-of-range

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [altitude](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#altitude)
- Automatic fix: no

An altitude should be a realistic value.

This rule reports altitudes that are probably wrong:

- an altitude above FL660 (66000 ft). Airspace limits are almost never that high. Files often use a value such as "FL999" to mean "no upper limit". Write "AH UNL" for this.
- a negative height above the ground (AGL) or a negative pressure altitude (STD),
- an altitude below 1500 ft under mean sea level (AMSL).

Correct:

```
AH UNL
```

Incorrect:

```
AH FL999
```

### altitude-zero-agl

- Severity: **warning**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [al-lower-altitude-limit](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#al-lower-altitude-limit)
- Automatic fix: --fix writes "AL GND".

For a lower limit at the ground, write "AL GND".

The specification says: for areas that extend to the ground, use GND, without an altitude. "AL 0 FT AGL" means the same, but "AL GND" is the form of the specification.

If the value also has an error, another rule reports it with the same advice, and this rule does not report it. "AL 0 AGL" (no unit) is reported by altitude-unit-missing. "AL 0 FT GND" and "AL 0 SFC" are reported by altitude-unknown-reference.

Correct:

```
AL GND
```

Incorrect:

```
AL 0 FT AGL
```

### altitude-lower-not-below-upper

- Severity: **error**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [al-lower-altitude-limit](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#al-lower-altitude-limit)
- Automatic fix: no

The lower limit (AL) must be below the upper limit (AH).

AH is the ceiling and AL is the floor of the airspace. The floor must be below the ceiling. A lower limit equal to the upper limit is not valid, because the airspace then has no height. Often the AH and AL values are swapped.

The limits can only be compared when they use the same kind of reference. openair-lint compares them when both are AMSL (MSL counts as AMSL), both are AGL (GND counts as 0 FT AGL), or both are standard pressure (FL and STD: "9500 FT STD" is the same as FL95). It converts metres to feet. It does not compare AMSL with AGL or with flight levels, because the difference depends on the terrain and on the air pressure.

Correct:

```
AH FL95
AL FL65
```

Incorrect:

```
AH FL65
AL FL95
```

### altitude-unit-metres

- Severity: **info**
- Versions: 2.1, 3.0
- Specification: [altitude](https://github.com/naviter/seeyou_file_formats/blob/main/OpenAir_File_Format_Support.md#altitude)
- Automatic fix: no

Feet (FT) are recommended for altitudes. Metres (M) are allowed.

The specification says: altitude is specified in feet FT (recommended) or in meters M. An altitude in metres is valid. This rule is info and not a warning, because the specification allows both units and only recommends one of them.

Write the published value. If the published value is in metres, keep it in metres. A conversion to feet can change the limit by rounding.

Correct:

```
AH 5000 FT AMSL
```

Incorrect:

```
AH 1500 M AMSL
```
